issues.title: Flash attention backend type not stored in inductor cache, causes silent usage of wrong backend
issues.author: ad8e
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

```py
"""Minimal repro: Inductor's FX graph cache key ignores the SDPA backend selection.

A `torch.compile`'d `F.scaled_dot_product_attention` lowers to a backend-specific
aten op (`_scaled_dot_product_flash_attention` vs `_scaled_dot_product_cudnn_attention`),
chosen from the active SDPA backend selection at compile time. But the on-disk FX
graph cache key does NOT include that selection -- neither the
`torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel(...)` context manager nor the
`torch.backends.cuda.enable_*_sdp(...)` flags.

So the first process to compile a given graph populates the cache, and later
processes sharing TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR get a cache hit and silently reuse that
backend regardless of what they request. Below, one process compiles the graph
under flash, then a second process requesting cuDNN reuses the cached flash
artifact -- you can see it lower to `_scaled_dot_product_flash_attention` despite
asking for cuDNN. Setting TORCHINDUCTOR_FORCE_DISABLE_CACHES=1 makes the second
process correctly lower to cuDNN, confirming the FX graph cache key is the culprit.

We detect the selected backend by capturing Inductor's `output_code` log and
reading the aten op name from the generated wrapper -- this is the compile-time
selection itself, not a heuristic on runtime kernel names. (Note: don't sniff the
profiler's CUDA kernel names for this -- cuDNN's SDPA kernel on sm100 is named
`cudnn_generated_..._flash_fprop_...`, i.e. it contains the substring "flash",
which trips up naive name matching.)

Run:    python compile_sdpa_cache_repro.py
Compare: TORCHINDUCTOR_FORCE_DISABLE_CACHES=1 python compile_sdpa_cache_repro.py
Requires a CUDA GPU with both flash and cuDNN SDPA backends (sm80+).
"""

import io
import logging
import os
import re
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile

import torch
from torch.nn.attention import SDPBackend, sdpa_kernel


def f(q, k, v):
    return torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)


def worker(backend: str) -> None:
    """Compile `f` under one SDPA backend; print the aten op Inductor selected."""
    bk = {"flash": SDPBackend.FLASH_ATTENTION, "cudnn": SDPBackend.CUDNN_ATTENTION}[backend]

    # Capture Inductor's generated wrapper code so we can read the selected op.
    buf = io.StringIO()
    torch._logging.set_logs(output_code=True)
    logging.getLogger("torch._inductor").addHandler(logging.StreamHandler(buf))

    # Match how a real consumer selects cuDNN: flip the global enable flag AND
    # enter the sdpa_kernel context. (Neither is part of the FX graph cache key.)
    torch.backends.cuda.enable_cudnn_sdp(backend == "cudnn")
    fc = torch.compile(f, dynamic=False)
    q = k = v = torch.randn(2, 8, 1024, 64, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
    with sdpa_kernel(bk):
        fc(q, k, v)
        torch.cuda.synchronize()

    ops = set(re.findall(r"_scaled_dot_product_(\w+?)_attention", buf.getvalue()))
    print(f"OP={ops.pop() if len(ops) == 1 else sorted(ops)}")


def spawn(backend: str, cache_dir: str) -> str:
    """Run a worker in a fresh process sharing `cache_dir`; return the op it lowered to."""
    env = {**os.environ, "TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR": cache_dir}
    out = subprocess.run([sys.executable, __file__, backend], env=env, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
    return next(line[3:] for line in out.splitlines() if line.startswith("OP="))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) > 1:  # worker mode
        worker(sys.argv[1])
        sys.exit()

    print("torch", torch.__version__, "| cuda", torch.version.cuda, "|", torch.cuda.get_device_name())
    print("TORCHINDUCTOR_FORCE_DISABLE_CACHES =", os.environ.get("TORCHINDUCTOR_FORCE_DISABLE_CACHES", "<unset>"))
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as cache_dir:  # one shared, initially-empty cache
        flash_op = spawn("flash", cache_dir)  # populates the cache
        cudnn_op = spawn("cudnn", cache_dir)  # should lower to cudnn; gets a cache hit instead
    print(f"process 1 requested flash -> lowered to {flash_op}")
    print(f"process 2 requested cudnn -> lowered to {cudnn_op}")
    assert flash_op == "flash", f"expected flash, got {flash_op}"
    if cudnn_op == "flash":
        print("\nBUG: the cuDNN process reused the cached flash artifact. "
              "Rerun with TORCHINDUCTOR_FORCE_DISABLE_CACHES=1 and process 2 correctly lowers to cudnn.")
    else:
        print(f"\nNo bug here: process 2 lowered to {cudnn_op} (cache disabled, or the cache key has been fixed).")
```

### Error logs

```
kevin@kevin-b200-0:/mnt/clusterstorage/workspace/kevin/ml-monorepo/chadfusion$ python compile_sdpa_cache_repro.py 
torch 2.12.0 | cuda 13.2 | NVIDIA B200

issues.title: Inductor pointwise operations slower with TMA than without
issues.author: riccardofelluga
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Enabling Inductor's generic pointwise TMA path with
`torch._inductor.config.triton.use_tensor_descriptor=True` makes this simple
SiLU kernel slower than the default `torch.compile` path on both B200 and H100.

This is due to descriptor setup overhead: the generic codegen path builds
TMA tensor descriptors inside the generated Triton kernel, so each CTA pays
descriptor construction cost. For a simple memory-bound pointwise op, that
overhead can outweigh any benefit from TMA loads.

## Repro


```python
"""
Run:
  python repro_inductor_tma_slowdown.py
"""

import statistics

import torch
import torch._inductor.config as inductor_config


SHAPES = [
    (4096, 4096),
    (8192, 8192),
    (16384, 16384),
]


def compile_silu():
    return torch.compile(
        lambda x: torch.nn.functional.silu(x),
        mode="max-autotune-no-cudagraphs",
        fullgraph=True,
    )


def bench(fn, x, warmup=10, iters=100):
    for _ in range(warmup):
        fn(x)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()

    times_us = []
    for _ in range(iters):
        start = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
        end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
        start.record()
        fn(x)
        end.record()
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        times_us.append(start.elapsed_time(end) * 1000)
    return statistics.median(times_us)


if not torch.cuda.is_available():
    raise SystemExit("CUDA is required")

print(f"PyTorch: {torch.__version__}")
print(f"CUDA: {torch.version.cuda}")
print()
print("| Shape | default compile us | compile + TMA us | slowdown |")
print("|---|---:|---:|---:|")

for shape in SHAPES:
    x = torch.randn(shape, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)

    torch._dynamo.reset()
    inductor_config.triton.use_tensor_descriptor = False
    inductor_config.assume_aligned_inputs = False
    default = compile_silu()
    default(x)
    default_us = bench(default, x)

    torch._dynamo.reset()
    inductor_config.triton.use_tensor_descriptor = True
    inductor_config.assume_aligned_inputs = True
    tma = compile_silu()
    tma(x)
    tma_us = bench(tma, x)
    slowdown = tma_us / default_us

    m, n = shape
    print(f"| {m}x{n} | {default_us:.1f} | {tma_us:.1f} | {slowdown:.2f}x |")

```

The script compares the same bf16 SiLU workload in two modes:

1. Default `torch.compile`
2. `torch.compile` with `triton.use_tensor_descriptor=True`

It resets Dynamo before compiling each mode so the two paths do not share a
cached compiled graph.

## Results

### B200

| Shape | default compile us | compile + TMA us | slowdown |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 4096x4096 | 56.1 | 78.8 | 1.41x |
| 8192x8192 | 87.5 | 141.4 | 1.62x |
| 16384x16384 | 220.0 | 358.4 | 1.63x |

### H100

| Shape | default compile us | compile + TMA us | slowdown |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 4096x4096 | 52.4 | 72.3 | 1.38x |
| 8192x8192 | 117.8 | 140.2 | 1.19x |
| 16384x16384 | 380.9 | 433.9 | 1.14x |

## Proposed Direction

The TMA descriptor should be created once on the host and passed into the
kernel, instead of being rebuilt inside every CTA. Inductor already has
host-side TMA descriptor infrastructure for template paths; the gap is wiring
that approach into the generic pointwise codegen path.

issues.title: [vllm] [2.12 regression][Inductor] assert_size_stride (8192 vs 512) in BERT-with-rope AOT-compiled path for Nomic v2 MoE pooling model
issues.author: atalman
issues.body:
## Summary

On `torch==2.12.0` + `triton==3.7.0`, the Extended-Pooling pytest job for the `nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v2-moe` model fails inside an Inductor AOT-compiled forward with a runtime stride/shape assertion:

```
File "/root/.cache/vllm/torch_compile_cache/torch_aot_compile/<hash>/inductor_cache/ra/cra7eslwqvpfcdh65siik6ag5goi4wdpxi6ivjnoyjbr4zci2oje.py", line 664
    assert_size_stride(arg9_1, (512, 64), (64, 1))
AssertionError: expected size 8192==512, stride 64==64 at dim=0
This error most often comes from a incorrect fake (aka meta) kernel for a custom op.
```

The compiled function's entrypoint is `vllm/model_executor/models/bert_with_rope.py:476::forward`. The path is the `flashinfer_autotune → runner._dummy_run` kernel warmup that runs as part of `_initialize_kv_caches`.

The expected dim-0 size in the compiled artifact is 512 (the configured `max_model_len`) but the runtime input has dim-0 size 8192 — exactly 16× larger, consistent with an MoE expert-broadcast (Nomic v2 MoE has 16 experts) where the fake kernel for the MoE custom op declared the post-MoE shape as `(seq_len, hidden)` while the runtime allocation is `(seq_len * num_experts, hidden)`.

Inductor's hint about a wrong fake kernel matches the diagnosis in vllm-project/vllm#40960 / pytorch/pytorch#182328 (the gpt-oss `moe_forward` case) — likely a similar vLLM-side `register_fake` / `direct_register_custom_op` shape mismatch, specific to the Nomic v2 MoE path. **Root cause is probably in vLLM**, not torch.

## Environment

- `torch==2.12.0+cu130`
- `triton==3.7.0`
- `torchvision==0.27.0`
- CUDA 13.0
- GPU: H200 (Buildkite `h200-ci-6-3`)
- Python 3.12
- vLLM commit `d2792bf2088c` (PR vllm-project/vllm#42848)
- Model: `nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v2-moe`, `runner=pooling`, `max_model_len=512`, `dtype=auto` (downcast to fp16)

## Reproduction

```
pytest -x tests/models/language/pooling/test_nomic_max_model_len.py::test_use_rope_scaling_legal[model_info1]
```

`model_info1` selects `nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v2-moe`; the test instantiates `VllmRunner` with `hf_overrides={"rope_parameters": {"rope_theta": ..., "rope_type": "yarn", "factor": ...}}` and `max_model_len=512`. Crash happens during `flashinfer_autotune` warmup.

## Traceback (trimmed)

```
vllm/v1/engine/core.py:283 _initialize_kv_caches
  → vllm/v1/executor/abstract.py:124 initialize_from_config
    → vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:608 compile_or_warm_up_model
      → vllm/model_executor/warmup/kernel_warmup.py:133 flashinfer_autotune
        → runner._dummy_run
          → vllm/model_executor/models/bert_with_rope.py:476 forward
            → AOT compiled fn → Inductor output_code
              → assert_size_stride(arg9_1, (512, 64), (64, 1))
              AssertionError: expected size 8192==512, stride 64==64 at dim=0
```

## Diagnosis question

Is the `assert_size_stride` insertion behavior new in 2.12 for this code path (e.g. a `Tag.needs_fixed_stride_order` change that started routing the MoE expert-broadcast through the assertion)? If yes, vLLM should fix the fake kernel; this can be tracked vLLM-side and closed `not_planned` here. If the assertion existed before but the fake kernel was bypassed under 2.11, please confirm so we can prioritize the vLLM-side fake-impl fix.

## Links

- vLLM PR: vllm-project/vllm#42848
- Failing build: https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/66993#019e4286-221f-478d-b5ec-c27b1732d6a2
- Passing main baselines (torch 2.11): builds #66975, #66835, #66759 (job not present in #67062, #65912 shard)
- Related vLLM-side fake-kernel issue: pytorch/pytorch#182328
- Umbrella: pytorch/pytorch#180899

comments.body:
### Bisected to vLLM #41277 (Dynamic NTK rope cache); reproducible across builds

Update from the torch-2.12 branch CI triage.

**Bisect.** Last-good build [#66553](https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/66553) (`47af9e1`, 2026-05-16) **passed** this job; first-bad [#66993](https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/66993) (`d2792bf`, 2026-05-19) **failed** with the identical `expected size 8192==512`. The torch wheel is the same `2.12.0+cu130` in both, so the trigger is a vLLM commit in `47af9e1..d2792bf`:

> vLLM PR vllm-project/vllm#41277 "Fix error in Dynamic NTK scaling" (`117afeea4`, 2026-05-19)

It changes the Dynamic-NTK RoPE cos/sin cache length in `vllm/model_executor/layers/rotary_embedding/dynamic_ntk_scaling_rope.py`:

```diff
-        max_len = self.max_position_embeddings * self.scaling_factor
-        t = torch.arange(max_len, dtype=torch.float)            # old length: 8192
+        t = torch.arange(self.max_position_embeddings, ...)     # new length: 512
```

The cache moved from `max_position_embeddings * scaling_factor` (**8192**) to `max_position_embeddings` (**512**) - exactly the two numbers in the assertion. The same PR also rewrote `test_nomic_max_model_len.py` and the `get_rope` wiring. This suggests the `16x` factor here is the **rope (yarn) scaling factor**, not the MoE expert count - so the MoE-fake-kernel hypothesis in the description above may be a coincidence (16 experts vs 16x scaling).

**Reproducibility.** Identical signature on every torch-2.12 branch build since #41277: [#66993](https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/66993), [#67522](https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/67522), [#69268](https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/69268). **Passes on all 5 recent main (torch 2.11) Full CI builds**: 69423, 69310, 69146, 69110, 69077 - so #41277 alone is fine on 2.11; it only fails under torch 2.12's Inductor/AOT stride assertion. Note the asserted `arg9_1` is a top-level graph input (not a custom-op output), so the generic "incorrect fake kernel" hint is likely misleading.

Suggested next step: a revert-#41277 build on the 2.12 branch to confirm, and loop in the #41277 author.

## Summary

`tests/compile/test_aot_compile.py::test_standalone_compile_correctness` (a `compare_two_settings` test that boots two `RemoteOpenAIServer` subprocesses with OPT-125m) fails on torch 2.12 with the engine subprocess crashing immediately:

    assert not envs.VLLM_USE_MEGA_AOT_ARTIFACT or envs.VLLM_USE_STANDALONE_COMPILE, (
AssertionError: VLLM_USE_MEGA_AOT_ARTIFACT=1 requires VLLM_USE_STANDALONE_COMPILE=1
```

The vLLM precondition expects that whenever the test launches the second server with `VLLM_USE_MEGA_AOT_ARTIFACT=1`, `VLLM_USE_STANDALONE_COMPILE=1` is also set. In the same job, several other compile tests print Inductor warnings while still passing:

```

cannot save. Run with TORCH_LOGS=+torch._inductor.codecache to identify the issue
```

(`test_sym_size_whole_shape_boundary`, `test_shape_boundary_standalone_compile`, `test_sym_size_metadata_propagated`, … all PASS but log the warning.) That points at a torch 2.12 Inductor `standalone_compile` regression that is silently swallowed in the warmup tests but fatal in the AOT-correctness test that depends on the cached artifact being saved and reloaded.

## Environment

- `torch==2.12.0+cu130`
- `triton==3.7.0`
- `torchvision==0.27.0`
- CUDA 13.0
- GPU: H200 (Buildkite `h200-ci-3-19`)
- Python 3.12
- vLLM commit `d2792bf2088c` (PR vllm-project/vllm#42848)

```
pytest -x tests/compile/test_aot_compile.py::test_standalone_compile_correctness
```

The test calls `compare_two_settings(...)` which spawns two `RemoteOpenAIServer` subprocesses; the second subprocess sets `VLLM_USE_MEGA_AOT_ARTIFACT=1` and the engine asserts in `vllm/compilation/backends.py:97`.

## Failing test

`tests/compile/test_aot_compile.py::test_standalone_compile_correctness`

Two related questions:

1. Did the semantics of `VLLM_USE_STANDALONE_COMPILE` or the default behavior of `torch._inductor.standalone_compile.compile_fx_with_dynamo_aot` change in torch 2.12 such that vLLM's env-var precondition stopped holding under what was previously a valid combination? 2. The `standalone_compile artifact generation failed, cannot save` warnings appearing in the same job point at a torch-side codecache regression — is the failure to save the standalone artifact intentional in 2.12 (e.g. cache schema change), or a bug we should fix?

The warnings only appear on torch 2.12 — on torch 2.11 (same vLLM commits, all five recent main builds), this job passes with no such warnings and `test_standalone_compile_correctness` passes.

issues.title: [dynamo] set subclass overriding __iter__ gives wrong result for set comparison under torch.compile
issues.author: guilhermeleobas
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.compile` produces the wrong result when comparing a builtin `set` against a `set` subclass that overrides `__iter__`. CPython's `set` rich comparison operates on the internal C struct and ignores `__iter__`, but Dynamo materializes the subclass's items by iterating it in Python, so a "lying" `__iter__` corrupts the captured set contents.

```python
import torch


class MySet(set):
    def __iter__(self):
        return iter([99])  # lie


def fn(s1, s2):
    return s1 == s2


s1 = {1, 2, 3}
s2 = MySet({1, 2, 3})

print("eager:   ", fn(s1, s2))                                                  # True
print("compiled:", torch.compile(fn, backend="eager", fullgraph=True)(s1, s2))  # False
```

Output:

```
eager:    True
compiled: False
```

Eager returns `True` because `set.__eq__` compares the actual stored elements (`{1, 2, 3} == {1, 2, 3}`). Under `torch.compile`, Dynamo builds the `set` subclass's items via Python-level iteration (`list(...)` / `dict.fromkeys(...)`), which calls the overridden `__iter__` and captures `{99}` instead, so the comparison yields `False`.

issues.title: `torch.compile(mode='reduce-overhead')` fails when user model uses wait_stream to synchronize side work
issues.author: tfogal
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Under `mode='reduce-overhead'`, work issued inside a user-written side stream does not synchronize back to the main stream even if the user does so explicitly. This causes stream capture errors.

The code below results in a `cudaErrorStreamCaptureUnjoined` (i.e. "`torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: capturing stream has unjoined work`") error when run.

```python
import torch

side = torch.cuda.Stream()


def fn_no_sync(x):
    a = x * 2
    with torch.cuda.stream(side):
        b = a + 1
    return b


def fn_with_workaround(x):
    """The pattern PR #183711's test asserts inductor preserves."""
    a = x * 2
    side.wait_stream(torch.cuda.current_stream())
    with torch.cuda.stream(side):
        b = a + 1
    torch.cuda.current_stream().wait_stream(side)
    return b


def fn_eager(x):
    a = x * 2
    b = a + 1
    return b


def run(name, fn, mode, x):
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    opt = torch.compile(fn, mode=mode)
    out = None
    for _ in range(3):
        out = opt(x)
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
    expected = fn_eager(x)
    ok = torch.allclose(out, expected)
    print(f"  {name:35s} mode={mode!r:18s}  ok={ok}  "
          f"got={out[:3].tolist()}  expected={expected[:3].tolist()}")


x = torch.ones(1024, device="cuda")
print(f"torch={torch.__version__}, cuda={torch.version.cuda}")
print()
run("no sync",         fn_no_sync,         "default",         x)         # fine
run("with #183711 workaround", fn_with_workaround, "default",         x) # fine
run("with #183711 workaround", fn_with_workaround, "reduce-overhead", x) # fails

issues.title: [Inductor][TP] Micro-pipeline TP fusion misses slice/cat collective patterns
issues.author: sanketpurandare
issues.body:
### Minimal repro

```python
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
from torch.fx.experimental.proxy_tensor import make_fx
from torch.ops import _c10d_functional as c10d
from torch.distributed._functional_collectives import all_gather_tensor, reduce_scatter_tensor

# Run under a distributed test/process group. The important FX shapes are local;
# the same patterns appear after graph-level chunking around tensor-parallel
# all-gather and reduce-scatter collectives.

def ag_slice_cat_mm(x, w):
    y = all_gather_tensor(x, gather_dim=0, group=dist.group.WORLD)
    y = torch.cat([y.narrow(0, 0, 64), y.narrow(0, 64, 64)], dim=1)
    return y @ w

def mm_slice_cat_rs(x, w):
    y = x @ w
    y = torch.cat([y.narrow(1, 0, 8), y.narrow(1, 8, 8)], dim=0)
    return reduce_scatter_tensor(y, "avg", scatter_dim=0, group=dist.group.WORLD)

# micro_pipeline_tp_pass should recognize these as all-gather+matmul and
# matmul+reduce-scatter fusion opportunities, but today the slice/cat
# reassembly hides the collective from the existing pattern matcher.
```

### Issue

Graph-level chunking can introduce a slice/cat reassembly around collective results or inputs while preserving the same logical tensor value consumed by tensor-parallel matmuls. The micro-pipeline TP pass currently recognizes direct all-gather/matmul and matmul/reduce-scatter shapes, but it misses these slice/cat forms.

### Expected behavior

The TP micro-pipeline pass should fuse all-gather+matmul and matmul+reduce-scatter when the extra slice/cat nodes only reassemble the collective value into the layout expected by the matmul/reduce-scatter pattern.

### Actual behavior

The pass leaves the all-gather or reduce-scatter unfused, which regresses the generated graph for chunked tensor-parallel workloads.

### Suggested fix

Extend the existing pattern detection helpers to recognize the slice/cat collective forms, preserve the same safety checks around matmul users, and erase only the matched reassembly nodes after replacing the fused pattern.

issues.title: [torch.compile] Clarification/regression: Dynamo cache lookup guard eval is much slower in 2.12 vs 2.7 after `inline_inbuilt_nn_modules` became always True
issues.author: mihudaner
issues.body: ### 🐛 Describe the bug We are investigating a TorchDynamo cache lookup / guard evaluation performance regression when moving a large inference model from PyTorch 2.7 to a 2.12-based build. This is not currently a correctness issue. The compiled model runs, but the runtime overhead before entering compiled regions is noticeably higher. From `TORCH_LOGS="+guards"` and local profiling, the hot frame guard evaluation / cache lookup cost increased from roughly 1 ms in 2.7 to roughly 3-4 ms in 2.12 for our large decoder-style inference workload. We also noticed that `torch._dynamo.config.inline_inbuilt_nn_modules` is deprecated in newer PyTorch and effectively always True: ```python inline_inbuilt_nn_modules = Config( default=True, justknob="pytorch/compiler:inline_inbuilt_nn_modules", deprecated=True, deprecation_message="does not do anything, inline_inbuilt_nn_modules is always True", ) ``` The related commit message says: ```text inline_inbuilt_nn_modules has defaulted to True and the False path is legacy. This makes the config a no-op (always True), emits a deprecation warning when users set it to False, and removes all dead False-path code from runtime. ``` However, we could not find a detailed public issue or design note explaining the full motivation and expected behavior changes from this deprecation. We would like to confirm whether the cache lookup / guard eval regression we observe is expected, and what guard strategy changes may explain it. ### Error logs No Python exception is required to reproduce the performance issue. Representative guard log summary: ### Versions 2.7.1 and 2.12.0 #### Observed behavior For the same large inference workload and similar Dynamo configs: ```python torch._dynamo.config.guard_nn_modules = False torch._dynamo.config.inline_inbuilt_nn_modules = True ``` we observed approximately: ```text PyTorch 2.7: hot frame Guard eval latency: ~1.36 ms PyTorch 2.12: hot frame Guard eval latency: ~5.65 ms ``` The additional 2.12 `LAMBDA_GUARD`s appear In 2.7, similar object aliasing relations were logged as `OBJECT_ALIASING`, for example: ```text OBJECT_ALIASING: L['self']._modules['layers']._modules['0'].stream_prefetch is ... ``` #### Minimal reproducer direction We can provide a small reproducer that imitates the workload pattern: 1. Many repeated `nn.Module` layers. 2. Repeated module attributes used in shape computations, such as `top_k`, `spec_len`, `block_size`, `num_heads`, `head_dim`. 3. Module tensor attributes similar to `block_table`, `fa_norm_residual`, `cur_topk_list`. 4. Shared Python objects across layers to trigger alias identity guards. #### Questions 1. What was the full motivation for deprecating `torch._dynamo.config.inline_inbuilt_nn_modules` and making it effectively always True? 2. Is the intended guidance that users should no longer try `inline_inbuilt_nn_modules=False` as a performance workaround? 3. Besides `inline_inbuilt_nn_modules` becoming deprecated/no-op, what other Dynamo guard or cache lookup changes between 2.7 and 2.12 could increase runtime guard eval / cache lookup overhead for large inference graphs? 4. If no config can safely recover 2.7-like lookup overhead in 2.12, what is the recommended mitigation for large repeated-module inference models? Should users refactor code to avoid reading Python/module attributes inside compiled regions, or is there a compiler-side way to reduce repeated guards? cc @ezyang @gchanan @kadeng @msaroufim @chauhang @penguinwu @voznesenskym @EikanWang @jgong5 @Guobing-Chen @XiaobingSuper @zhuhaozhe @blzheng @wenzhe-nrv @jiayisunx @amjames @jataylo @azahed98

issues.title: [Inductor][CPU][bf16] Gradient mismatch in F.margin_ranking_loss backward with bfloat16 tensors and float scalar
issues.author: xyt66665000
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

There is a gradient mismatch between Eager mode and `torch.compile` (Inductor) when running `F.margin_ranking_loss` backward with `bfloat16` tensors and a Python `float` scalar as the `margin`. 

In Eager mode, the gradient propagates correctly (producing non-zero values), but in Inductor, the gradient becomes completely zero. This discrepancy occurs at the boundary condition where the loss evaluates to exactly `0.0` depending on how the Python float scalar is promoted or cast during the computation.

This reproducer uses CPU tensors. I also tested the same reproducer on CUDA, where Eager and Inductor both produce zero gradients, so the mismatch appears to be CPU-specific.

**To Reproduce**

```python
import torch

def test_margin_ranking_loss_boundary():
    x_val = 1.703125
    margin_val = 1.7 

    input1 = torch.tensor([x_val, x_val], dtype=torch.bfloat16, requires_grad=True)
    input2 = torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0], dtype=torch.bfloat16, requires_grad=True)
    target = torch.tensor([1.0, 1.0], dtype=torch.bfloat16)

    def fn(x, y, t):
        return torch.nn.functional.margin_ranking_loss(x, y, t, margin=margin_val, reduction='mean')

    loss_eager = fn(input1, input2, target)
    loss_eager.backward()
    grad_eager = input1.grad.clone()
    print(f"Eager grad:    {grad_eager.tolist()}") 
    
    input1.grad.zero_()
    input2.grad.zero_()

    opt_fn = torch.compile(fn, backend='inductor')
    loss_inductor = opt_fn(input1, input2, target)
    loss_inductor.backward()
    grad_inductor = input1.grad.clone()
    print(f"Inductor grad: {grad_inductor.tolist()}") 
    
    assert torch.allclose(grad_eager, grad_inductor), "Gradient mismatch at boundary due to precision loss!"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_margin_ranking_loss_boundary()
```

**Output:**
```text
(torch-nightly) xyt19@Oasis:/tmp$ python bug.py
Eager grad:    [-0.5, -0.5]
Inductor grad: [0.0, 0.0]
Traceback (most recent call last):

    test_margin_ranking_loss_boundary()

    assert torch.allclose(grad_eager, grad_inductor), "Gradient mismatch at boundary due to precision loss!"
AssertionError: Gradient mismatch at boundary due to precision loss!
```

**Expected behavior**
`torch.compile` should yield the same gradients as Eager mode for `bfloat16` inputs interacting with `float` scalars, maintaining consistent type promotion and precision semantics.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

## 🐛 Bug Report

### Description
PyTorch Dynamo compilation fails when processing `aten.embedding.default` operations that involve tensors on different devices (`cpu` and `meta`). The error occurs during FakeTensor propagation in the compilation phase, while normal eager execution works correctly.
code:
```
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class DotProductAttention(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self, embed_size, heads):
        super(DotProductAttention, self).__init__()
        self.embed_size = embed_size
        self.heads = heads
        self.head_dim = embed_size // heads
        assert self.head_dim * heads == embed_size
        self.values = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size)
        self.keys = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size)
        self.queries = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size)
        self.fc_out = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size)

    def forward(self, values, keys, queries, mask=None):
        N = queries.shape[0]
        (value_len, key_len, query_len) = (values.shape[1], keys.shape[1], queries.shape[1])
        values = self.values(values)
        keys = self.keys(keys)
        queries = self.queries(queries)
        values = values.reshape(N, value_len, self.heads, self.head_dim)
        keys = keys.reshape(N, key_len, self.heads, self.head_dim)
        queries = queries.reshape(N, query_len, self.heads, self.head_dim)
        energy = torch.einsum('nqhd,nkhd->nhqk', [queries, keys])
        if mask is not None:
            energy = energy.masked_fill(mask == 0, float('-1e20'))
        attention = torch.softmax(energy / self.embed_size ** (1 / 2), dim=3)
        out = torch.einsum('nhql,nlhd->nqhd', [attention, values])
        out = out.reshape(N, query_len, self.heads * self.head_dim)
        out = self.fc_out(out)
        return out

class DotProductAttentionBlock(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self, embed_size, heads, forward_expansion, dropout):
        super(DotProductAttentionBlock, self).__init__()
        self.attention = DotProductAttention(embed_size, heads)
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(embed_size)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(embed_size)
        self.feed_forward = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(embed_size, forward_expansion * embed_size), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(forward_expansion * embed_size, embed_size))
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)

    def forward(self, value, key, query, mask=None):
        attention = self.attention(value, key, query, mask)
        x = self.dropout(self.norm1(attention + query))
        forward = self.feed_forward(x)
        out = self.dropout(self.norm2(forward + x))
        return out

class DotProductAttentionDNN(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self, input_size, embed_size, num_layers, heads, forward_expansion, output_size, dropout, max_length):
        super(DotProductAttentionDNN, self).__init__()
        self.embed_size = embed_size
        self.word_embedding = nn.Embedding(input_size, embed_size)
        self.position_embedding = nn.Embedding(max_length, embed_size)
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([DotProductAttentionBlock(embed_size, heads, forward_expansion, dropout) for _ in range(num_layers)])
        self.fc = nn.Linear(embed_size, output_size)
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)

    def forward(self, x, mask=None):
        (N, seq_length) = x.shape
        positions = torch.arange(0, seq_length).expand(N, seq_length).to('meta')
        out = self.dropout(self.word_embedding(x) + self.position_embedding(positions))
        for layer in self.layers:
            out = layer(out, out, out, mask)
        out = self.fc(out)
        return out

def get_default_model():
    return DotProductAttentionDNN(input_size=1000, embed_size=128, num_layers=2, heads=4, forward_expansion=2, output_size=10, dropout=0.1, max_length=20)

def get_sample_inputs(batch_size=2, seq_length=10):
    x = torch.randint(0, 1000, (batch_size, seq_length))
    mask = torch.ones(batch_size, 1, 1, seq_length)
    return (x, mask)

def run_inference(model, x, mask):
    with torch.no_grad():
        output = model(x, mask)
    return output


def main():
    model = get_default_model()
    model.eval()
    (x, mask) = get_sample_inputs()

    output_normal = run_inference(model, x, mask)
    print('Normal inference successful')
    print(f'Output shape: {output_normal.shape}')

    try:
        compiled_model = torch.compile(model)
        compiled_model.eval()
        output_compiled = run_inference(compiled_model, x, mask)
        print('Compiled inference successful')
        print(f'Compiled output shape: {output_compiled.shape}')

        diff = torch.abs(output_normal - output_compiled).max().item()
        print(f'Output difference: {diff:.6f}')

    except Exception as exception:
        print("Compilation failed:", exception)

    print(f'Model parameters: {sum((p.numel() for p in model.parameters()))}')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

issues.title: Inductor compile-worker subprocess+fork pool initializes CUDA in parent before fork, breaking with upstream Triton 3.7.0+
issues.author: FindHao
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug


Inductor's default compile-worker pool initializes CUDA in the manager process (via `pre_fork_setup()`) and then `fork()`s workers. CUDA contexts are process-local, so the forked workers inherit invalid state. Upstream Triton nightly 3.7.0+'s new `_cuda_driver_is_active()` probe calls `cuInit(0)` in the worker, gets `CUDA_ERROR_NOT_INITIALIZED`, and Triton's driver discovery raises `RuntimeError: 0 active drivers ([])`. Reproduces with **default PyTorch settings** as soon as a user installs the upstream `triton` wheel instead of `pytorch-triton`.

## To Reproduce

Self-contained reproducer (no PyTorch-side env tweaks — just the upstream Triton wheel and the default inductor worker pool):

```python
"""repro_inductor_triton_fork_cuda.py"""
import os

# Force inductor to use its compile-worker pool (>1).
# On most machines TORCHINDUCTOR_COMPILE_THREADS is already > 1 by default.
os.environ["TORCHINDUCTOR_COMPILE_THREADS"] = "4"

import torch
import triton


def _a(x): return (x * 2 + 1).relu().sum()
def _b(x): return (x.sin() + x.cos()).pow(2).mean()
def _c(x): return torch.softmax(x @ x.T, dim=-1).sum()
def _d(x): return (x.tanh() * x.exp().clamp(max=10.0)).log1p().mean()


def main():
    print(f"torch  = {torch.__version__}")
    print(f"triton = {triton.__version__}")
    x = torch.randn(2048, 2048, device="cuda")
    for fn in (_a, _b, _c, _d):
        torch.compile(fn, dynamic=False, fullgraph=True)(x)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print("ALL OK")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

### Setup

```bash
pip install --pre torch torchvision torchaudio \
    --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/cu130
pip uninstall -y triton pytorch-triton
pip install --index-url \
    https://aiinfra.pkgs.visualstudio.com/PublicPackages/_packaging/Triton-Nightly/pypi/simple/ \
    "triton==3.7.0+git40e899b0"

rm -rf ~/.triton/cache /tmp/torchinductor_$USER
python repro_inductor_triton_fork_cuda.py
```

### Necessary conditions (all required)

- Upstream NVIDIA Triton wheel (`3.7.0+git40e899b0` confirmed; any version where `_cuda_driver_is_active()` calls `cuInit` is suspect)
- `TORCHINDUCTOR_COMPILE_THREADS > 1` (default on most machines)
- Cold `~/.triton/cache` (with warm cache the generated kernel is loaded directly without invoking `set_driver_to_gpu` in the worker)
- Cold `/tmp/torchinductor_$USER` (same reason)
- ≥ 3 distinct `torch.compile` units (race; 4+ is 100%)

## Expected behavior

`ALL OK`.

## Actual behavior

```
torch._inductor.exc.InductorError: SubprocException: An exception occurred in a subprocess:
...
  File ".../triton/runtime/driver.py", line 20, in _create_driver
    raise RuntimeError(f"{len(active_drivers)} active drivers ({active_drivers}). There should only be one.")
RuntimeError: 0 active drivers ([]). There should only be one.
```

## Root cause

```
parent (user script)
  └─ subprocess.Popen(...) → manager        # SubprocPool, default TORCHINDUCTOR_WORKER_START=subprocess
       torch/_inductor/compile_worker/__main__.py:
         line 30:  import triton            # preload in parent
         line 68:  pre_fork_setup()
                       → caching_device_properties()
                       → Worker.get_device_properties()
                       → INITIALIZES CUDA DRIVER STATE in manager     ← the anti-pattern
       then SubprocPool fork()s N workers
       (--kind=fork is the hard-coded default SubprocKind.FORK in
        torch/_inductor/compile_worker/subproc_pool.py:135)
       └─ forked worker
            inherits broken-after-fork CUDA state
            first line of inductor-generated kernel module is:
                triton_helpers.set_driver_to_gpu()
            → DriverConfig.active → DriverConfig.default → _create_driver()
              → for backend in backends.values(): backend.driver.is_active()
                → NVIDIA backend: _cuda_driver_is_active()
                   ctypes.CDLL("libcuda.so.1")        OK
                   cuInit(0)                           → rc=3  (NOT_INITIALIZED)
                   return False
              → active_drivers == []
            → RuntimeError("0 active drivers ([])")
```

Verified by patching `_cuda_driver_is_active` to log:

```
[pid=PARENT  argv=[repro.py]]                                   cuInit(0) rc=0  RESULT=True   # parent OK
[pid=MANAGER argv=[.../compile_worker/__main__.py, --kind=fork]] PATCH installed              # patch loaded in manager
[pid=WORKER  ppid=MANAGER ...]                                   cuInit(0) rc=3  RESULT=False # forked worker fails
```
Related triton PR:
https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/9578

### Versions

## Versions

```
python  3.14

issues.title: `torch.compile` produces wrong results when `F.layer_norm` is fused with `reciprocal`/`rsqrt` epilogue
issues.author: wuyii8941
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug


## Summary

When Inductor fuses `F.layer_norm` with a subsequent division-like pointwise op (`reciprocal`, `rsqrt`, `1/sqrt`), the generated kernel produces significantly wrong results. Each op alone compiles correctly; only the fused combination triggers the bug. `aot_eager` produces correct results, confirming this is an Inductor codegen issue.

## Minimal reproducer

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

x = torch.randn(64, 128, device='cuda')

def fn(x):
    return torch.reciprocal(torch.abs(F.layer_norm(x, [128])) + 1e-6)

eager = fn(x)

torch._dynamo.reset()
aot = torch.compile(fn, backend='aot_eager')(x)

torch._dynamo.reset()
compiled = torch.compile(fn, backend='inductor')(x)

print(f"eager vs aot_eager: {(eager - aot).abs().max().item():.4e}")    # 0.0000e+00
print(f"eager vs inductor:  {(eager - compiled).abs().max().item():.4e}")  # ~9e-01
```

## Affected ops (epilogue after `layer_norm`)

| Epilogue op | Triggers? | Max diff |
|-------------|-----------|----------|
| `reciprocal` | Yes | ~80 (shape dependent) |
| `rsqrt` | Yes | ~877 (with cummax prefix) |
| `1/sqrt` (manual) | Yes | ~0.05 |
| `exp` | No | ~7e-6 |
| `tanh` | No | ok |

## Trigger conditions

- **Op pattern**: `F.layer_norm(x, [N])` followed by `reciprocal`, `rsqrt`, or `1/sqrt`
- **Shape dependent**: larger tensors trigger more reliably; small tensors (e.g., `(2, 256)`) may not trigger
- **dtype**: primarily float32; float16 also affected; float64 and bfloat16 appear unaffected
- **Backend**: Inductor only; `aot_eager` is correct
- **Each op alone is correct**: `layer_norm` alone is correct (diff ~7e-7), `reciprocal`/`rsqrt` alone on LN output is correct (diff = 0)
- **Manual normalization does not trigger**: `x / sqrt(mean(x^2) + eps)` + `rsqrt` is fine — only `F.layer_norm` triggers

## Amplified by upstream scan ops

When `cummax`/`cummin`/`cumsum` precedes the pattern, the error is amplified dramatically because the scan output distribution differs from random normal:

```python
x = torch.randn(68, 4, 14, 9, device='cuda')

def fn(x):
    t = torch.cummax(x, dim=-1)[0]         # scan op
    t = F.layer_norm(t, [9])                # layer_norm
    return torch.rsqrt(torch.abs(t) + 1e-6) # rsqrt epilogue

eager = fn(x)
torch._dynamo.reset()
compiled = torch.compile(fn, backend='inductor')(x)
print((eager - compiled).abs().max().item())  # ~877
```

## Shape sensitivity

```
# reciprocal(|LN(x)| + eps), varying shape:
(32, 64)      → diff=0.011
(64, 128)     → diff=0.82
(32, 32, 32)  → diff=81
(8, 4, 14, 9) → diff=0.077
```



### Versions


## Environment

- PyTorch: 2.13.0.dev20260601+cu126
- GPU: NVIDIA Tesla T4 (CUDA 12.6)
- OS: Linux

issues.title: [Inductor] Checkpointed reductions can choose different configs between forward and recompute
issues.author: sanketpurandare
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Activation-checkpointed reductions compiled by Inductor can pick different reduction/autotuning configs for the original forward and the checkpoint recompute. When the reduction feeds a discrete downstream decision, low-bit drift between the original forward and recompute can change routing/count logic even though the model code is deterministic.

The important part is that the original forward graph and the AC recompute graph are compiled independently. The recompute graph can materialize backward-needed outputs and therefore have different register pressure. With dynamic R-block selection enabled, that can select a different reduction tree than the original forward.

A minimal repro is below. It uses only PyTorch APIs: `torch.compile`, non-reentrant `checkpoint`, an RMSNorm-like reduction, and a custom compare op that records the original forward output and compares it with the recompute output. No randomness or nondeterminism is injected after the input is created.

```python
import os

import torch
from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint


torch.manual_seed(0)
torch.set_default_device("cuda")

seen = []


@torch.library.custom_op("ac_repro::compare", mutates_args=())
def compare(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    # First real call is the original forward. The second real call is the
    # checkpoint recompute during backward.
    if len(seen) == 0:
        seen.append(x.detach().clone())
    else:
        ref = seen[0]
        if not torch.equal(ref, x):
            diff = (ref.float() - x.float()).abs()
            idx = diff.argmax()
            raise RuntimeError(
                "checkpoint recompute mismatch: "
                f"max_abs={diff.max().item()} "
                f"ref={ref.flatten()[idx].item()} "
                f"got={x.flatten()[idx].item()} "
                f"dynamic_rblock={os.environ.get('TORCHINDUCTOR_DYNAMIC_SCALE_RBLOCK', '<default>')}"
            )
    return x


@compare.register_fake
def _(x):
    return torch.empty_like(x)


def setup_context(ctx, inputs, output):
    pass


def backward(ctx, grad):
    return grad


compare.register_autograd(backward, setup_context=setup_context)


def rmsnorm_like(x):
    # Reduction whose exact low bits can depend on the selected reduction tree.
    scale = torch.rsqrt((x.float() * x.float()).mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-6)
    y = x * scale.to(x.dtype)
    return torch.ops.ac_repro.compare.default(y)


def fn(x):
    y = checkpoint(rmsnorm_like, x, use_reentrant=False)
    return y.square().sum()


x = torch.randn(2048, 4096, dtype=torch.bfloat16, requires_grad=True)
compiled = torch.compile(fn, fullgraph=True)
loss = compiled(x)
loss.backward()
print("passed")
```

On an affected Blackwell/GB200-style backend, this fails before any router/topk/count logic is involved, with the compare op reporting a bf16 mismatch between the original forward and checkpoint recompute output.

A workaround is to disable dynamic R-block selection:

```bash
TORCHINDUCTOR_DYNAMIC_SCALE_RBLOCK=0 python repro.py
```

With that setting, the repro passes in the same environment.

This was originally noticed in TorchTitan full activation checkpointing, where the low-bit reduction drift later surfaced as a downstream `repeat_interleave(output_size=...)` mismatch in MoE routing/count handling: https://github.com/pytorch/torchtitan/issues/3336

### Versions

Observed on a recent PyTorch nightly/source build with CUDA on an affected Blackwell/GB200-style backend. The issue appears tied to Inductor dynamic R-block autotuning for independently compiled checkpoint forward/recompute reductions rather than Python-level nondeterminism.

issues.title: torch 2.12 regression: torch.compile thread-local config - even backward thread has separate config
issues.author: dxqb
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Since https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/173568 torch dynamo config is thread-local.
`torch._dynamo.config.cache_size_limit` default is 8, which is quite low if you have a couple of different shapes in a transformer. with `fullgraph=True`, this is a failure. without it, it executes code in eager mode when compilation was intended.

setting this value for each thread still seems reasonable, even though it is a breaking change that wasn't documented, I think. However, not even that is enough because the backward thread, launched by torch internally, has its own dynamo config.

If the breaking change was intended, I think at least the backward thread should copy its dynamo config from the thread that launches it.

AI-generated repro code:
```
# Repro: torch._dynamo.config.recompile_limit set in the calling thread does not apply
# to compilations triggered on autograd worker threads (activation checkpoint recomputation).
#
# Phase 1: limit raised in the main thread only (the documented way) -> hard failure in backward.
# Phase 2: limit additionally raised inside the checkpointed function, which also runs on the
#          autograd worker thread during recomputation -> all shapes succeed.
import threading

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint


class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = nn.Linear(8, 8)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.linear(x)


def run(set_limit_in_checkpointed_function):
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    # the documented way to raise the limit (per the FailOnRecompileLimitHit hint and the
    # recompilation programming-model docs) — a ContextVar set, visible in this thread only
    torch._dynamo.config.recompile_limit = 8192

    block = Block().cuda()
    # dynamic=False makes each input shape a distinct specialization, like shape-bucketing
    # workloads; backend="eager" keeps the repro fast (the limit check happens in dynamo)
    block.compile(fullgraph=True, backend="eager", dynamic=False)

    first_seen = {}

    def checkpointed(x):
        # runs in the main thread during forward (under no_grad), and on the autograd worker
        # thread during backward recomputation (with grad enabled)
        phase = "recompute" if torch.is_grad_enabled() else "forward"
        first_seen.setdefault(phase, (threading.get_native_id(), torch._dynamo.config.recompile_limit))
        if set_limit_in_checkpointed_function:
            torch._dynamo.config.recompile_limit = 8192
        return block(x)

    i = 0
    try:
        for i in range(1, 16):
            x = torch.randn(i, 8, device="cuda", requires_grad=True)
            checkpoint(checkpointed, x, use_reentrant=True).sum().backward()
        print("  all 15 shapes ok")
    except torch._dynamo.exc.FailOnRecompileLimitHit:
        print(f"  FailOnRecompileLimitHit in backward at shape ({i}, 8)")
    for phase, (tid, limit) in first_seen.items():
        print(f"  {phase:9} runs on thread {tid}, sees recompile_limit={limit} on first call")


print(f"main thread is {threading.get_native_id()}")
print("Phase 1 — limit set in main thread only (documented way):")
run(set_limit_in_checkpointed_function=False)
print("Phase 2 — limit additionally set inside the checkpointed function (reaches the autograd thread):")
run(set_limit_in_checkpointed_function=True)
```

Output:
```
Phase 1 — limit set in main thread only (documented way):
W0607 13:28:37.211000 441935 torch/_dynamo/convert_frame.py:1853] [0/9] torch._dynamo hit config.recompile_limit (8)
W0607 13:28:37.211000 441935 torch/_dynamo/convert_frame.py:1853] [0/9]    function: 'forward' (/home/claude/OneTrainer-lens/.lens-scratch/repro_recompile_limit.py:19)
W0607 13:28:37.211000 441935 torch/_dynamo/convert_frame.py:1853] [0/9]    last reason: 0/8: GLOBAL_STATE changed: grad_mode 
W0607 13:28:37.211000 441935 torch/_dynamo/convert_frame.py:1853] [0/9] To log all recompilation reasons, use TORCH_LOGS="recompiles".
W0607 13:28:37.211000 441935 torch/_dynamo/convert_frame.py:1853] [0/9] To diagnose recompilation issues, see https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/user_guide/torch_compiler/compile/programming_model.recompilation.html

issues.title: [Inductor][AOTI] codegen_symbol uses float reciprocal for integer dim recovery, silently corrupts dynamic batches when 1/K is not exactly representable in IEEE-754
issues.author: pjh4993
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch._inductor.aoti_compile_and_package` produces a package whose compiled forward silently returns wrong output rows whenever it has to recover a symbolic batch dim `s` from an input shape `K*s` and `(1.0/K)*K != 1.0` in IEEE-754 double precision. For non-power-of-2 `K` (e.g. `K=1496`, common in vision-tower token-grid shapes), the corruption hits at multiple runtime batch sizes — including the most degenerate case `bs=1`, which crashes inside `flash_attention` because the recovered batch evaluates to `0`.

Eager forward of the same `nn.Module` is correct at every batch on every version tested.

The bug is a composition of two PRs that are each individually correct:
- **#95698** (Mar 2023): made `CppPrinter._print_Rational` emit float division, intentionally, to fix `upsample_bilinear2d` / `upsample_nearest` dynamic-shape regressions (those ops need real fractional scale factors).
- **#146044** (Jan 2025): added composed-constraint dim recovery in `cpp_wrapper_cpu.py:codegen_symbol`, lowering `try_solve` results through the same `CppPrinter`. This routes integer dim recovery through the float-div printer.

Issue #145500 (the motivating bug for #146044) only used `K=2`, which is exactly representable, so the bug never surfaced in regression tests.


### Minimal reproducer (~30 lines, no extra deps)

```python
import os
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.export import Dim

D    = int(os.environ.get("D", 1280))
H    = int(os.environ.get("H", 16))
HD   = int(os.environ.get("HD", 80))
L    = int(os.environ.get("L", 1496))    # any K such that (1.0/K)*K != 1.0 reproduces
MAXN = int(os.environ.get("MAXN", 8))
assert D == H * HD


class M(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(D, 3 * D)
        self.out = nn.Linear(D, D)
    def forward(self, x, sizes):
        torch._check(x.shape[0] == sizes.shape[0] * L)
        x = x.unflatten(0, (-1, L))
        q, k, v = self.qkv(x).reshape(-1, L, 3, H, HD).permute(2, 0, 3, 1, 4).unbind(0)
        x = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(-1, L, D)
        return self.out(x.flatten(0, 1))


dev, dt = "cuda", torch.bfloat16
m = M().to(dev, dt).eval()
ex = (torch.randn(4 * L, D, device=dev, dtype=dt),
      torch.zeros(4, dtype=torch.long, device=dev))
ep = torch.export.export(m, ex, dynamic_shapes={"x": {0: Dim.AUTO}, "sizes": {0: Dim.AUTO}}, strict=True)
torch._inductor.aoti_compile_and_package(ep, package_path="/tmp/repro.pt2")
aoti = torch._inductor.aoti_load_package("/tmp/repro.pt2")

print(f"torch {torch.__version__}  example bs=4  L={L}  MAXN={MAXN}")
with torch.inference_mode():
    for bs in range(1, MAXN + 1):
        x = torch.randn(bs * L, D, device=dev, dtype=dt)
        s = torch.zeros(bs, dtype=torch.long, device=dev)
        eager_rows = m(x, s).shape[0]
        try:
            aoti_rows = aoti(x, s).shape[0]
            tag = "OK " if aoti_rows == eager_rows else "BAD"
        except Exception:
            aoti_rows, tag = "CRASH", "ERR"
        print(f"  bs={bs}: eager={eager_rows:4d}  aoti={aoti_rows!s:>5}  {tag}")
```

### Observed output (torch 2.9.1+cu128, RTX 3090)

```
torch 2.9.1+cu128  example bs=4  L=1496  MAXN=8
  bs=1: eager=1496  aoti=CRASH  ERR     ← flash_attn: "batch size must be positive" (recovered batch == 0)
  bs=2: eager=2992  aoti= 1496  BAD     ← one image short
  bs=3: eager=4488  aoti= 4488  OK
  bs=4: eager=5984  aoti= 4488  BAD     ← one image short
  bs=5: eager=7480  aoti= 7480  OK
  bs=6: eager=8976  aoti= 8976  OK
  bs=7: eager=10472  aoti=10472  OK
  bs=8: eager=11968  aoti=10472  BAD    ← one image short
```

Runtime warning that points at the root cause:

```
[W Resize.cpp:31] Warning: An output with one or more elements was resized since it had
shape [1496, 3840], which does not match the required output shape [2992, 3840].
```

`[L, 3*D]` = one image's worth of rows = AOTI's compile-time symbolic size for the QKV linear output. The runtime eager fallback resizes it because the true shape needs `bs*L` rows.

### Same bug reproduces on every version tested

| torch | bs=1 | bs=2 | bs=3 | bs=4 | bs=5 | bs=6 | bs=7 | bs=8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.8.0+cu128 | CRASH | bad | ✓ | bad | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | bad |
| 2.9.1+cu128 | CRASH | bad | ✓ | bad | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | bad |
| 2.12.0.dev20260408+cu128 | bad (0 rows) | bad | ✓ | bad | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | bad |

(2.12 nightly silently returns 0 rows at `bs=1` instead of crashing — same bug, slightly different surface.)

### Pure-Python predictor (no torch needed)

```python
def will_aoti_be_wrong_at(L: int, N: int) -> bool:
    return int((1.0 / L) * (N * L)) != N
```

Verified L-sensitivity (matches AOTI output exactly):

| L | rationale | predicted-bad bs∈[1..16] | observed-bad bs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1024 | `1/L = 2^-10` exactly representable | none | none ✓ |
| 1000 | `(1/L)*L` round-trips to exactly 1.0 | none | none ✓ |
| 1496 | `(1/L)*L = 0.9999999999999999` | {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} | {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} ✓ |
| 1500 | `(1/L)*L` round-trips to exactly 1.0 | none | none ✓ |

(`L=1496` is `34*44`, the Qwen2-VL 640×480 grid — a real shape, not contrived.)


### Root cause

#### Bad C++ in `wrapper.cpp:331` of the bs=1 crash trace

```cpp
int64_t s46 = (1.0/1496.0)*arg4_1_size_0;
```

This recovers the symbolic batch `s46` from `arg4_1.size(0) == 1496*s46` by floating-point reciprocal multiplication and truncation to `int64_t`. `1.0/1496.0` is not exactly representable in IEEE-754, so the product accumulates rounding error and truncates wrong for many inputs:

```
bs=1: q*1496  = 0.9999999999999999       → int64_t cast = 0  → flash_attn crash
bs=2: q*2992  = 1.9999999999999998       → 1                  → 1 image short
bs=3: q*4488  = exactly 3.0              → 3                  → ✓
bs=4: q*5984  = 3.9999999999999996       → 3                  → 1 image short
...
bs=8: q*11968 = 7.999999999999999        → 7                  → 1 image short
```

The wrong `s46` then propagates through every downstream buffer allocation (`{1496L*s46, 3840L}` for the QKV output, etc.).

#### Where this gets emitted

**`torch/_inductor/codegen/cpp_wrapper_cpu.py:331`** (`codegen_symbol`) recovers free symbols from input shapes:

```python
solution = try_solve(sympy.Eq(sym_or_exp, size_symbol), free_symbol)
if solution is not None:
    code.writeline(f"int64_t {free_symbol} = {cexpr(solution[1])};")
```

`try_solve` returns the algebraically correct `Mul(Rational(1, 1496), arg4_1_size_0)`. The expression then goes through `cexpr` (the `CppPrinter`), whose `_print_Rational` at **`torch/utils/_sympy/printers.py:400`** is documented to emit float division:

```python
def _print_Rational(self, expr):
    # Uses float constants to perform FP div
    if expr.q == 1:
        r = f"{expr.p}"
    else:
        r = f"{expr.p}.0/{expr.q}.0"
    return f"static_cast<{INDEX_TYPE}>({r})" if expr.is_integer else r
```

Combined with `ExprPrinter._print_Mul` (just `stringify(args, "*")`), `Mul(Rational(1, 1496), x)` lowers to `(1.0/1496.0)*x`. The outer `int64_t {free_symbol} = …;` then truncates the float to integer, dropping the rounding error into the symbol.

#### Why this was deliberate (and why it's still wrong here)

PR #95698 explicitly switched `_print_Rational` from integer division to FP division to fix `upsample_bilinear2d` / `upsample_nearest` dynamic shapes — those ops need real fractional scale factors `output_h / input_h`. The change was correct for upsample.

PR #146044 reused the same `cexpr` printer for integer dim recovery in AOTI, without realizing that the printer's `Rational` handling assumes float context. Issue #145500 (the motivating bug) used `K=2`, which is exactly representable in IEEE-754 — so the test never tripped the rounding path.


### Proposed fix

**Patch the call site, not the printer.** The type information ("I'm writing into `int64_t`") only exists at `codegen_symbol`; the printer is shared with upsample and other float-context callers.

```python
# torch/_inductor/codegen/cpp_wrapper_cpu.py:codegen_symbol

solution = try_solve(sympy.Eq(sym_or_exp, size_symbol), free_symbol)
if solution is not None:
    expr = solution[1]
    # try_solve returns Mul(Rational(1, K), x); rewrite to CleanDiv so cexpr
    # emits c10::div_floor_integer (exact integer division) instead of
    # (1.0/K.0)*x (FP reciprocal that loses precision when 1/K is not
    # exactly representable in IEEE-754).
    if isinstance(expr, sympy.Mul):
        coeff, rest = expr.as_coeff_Mul()
        if isinstance(coeff, sympy.Rational) and coeff.p == 1 and coeff.q != 1:
            from torch.utils._sympy.functions import CleanDiv
            expr = CleanDiv(rest, coeff.q)
    code.writeline(f"int64_t {free_symbol} = {cexpr(expr)};")
    bound_vars.add(free_symbol)
```

`CleanDiv` is torch's "exact integer division, divisor evenly divides" SymPy op — the constraint `K*s == size` from the export graph guarantees the divisibility. Its existing `CppPrinter._print_FloorDiv` (`printers.py:424`) emits:

```cpp
c10::div_floor_integer(static_cast<int64_t>(arg4_1_size_0), static_cast<int64_t>(1496L))
```

Why patch here and not `try_solve` or `_print_Rational`:

- `try_solve` has 15+ callers across torch (export, ShapeEnv, dynamo, range analysis). Most use the result purely symbolically — they shouldn't be perturbed.
- `_print_Rational` is load-bearing for upsample's fractional scale factors. Touching it regresses PR #95698's original motivation.
- Only `codegen_symbol` (and one or two similar call sites in `tiling_utils.py`) knows the lowering target is `int64_t`. Type-aware lowering belongs at the call site.

Patch was applied locally and verified.

### Verification (post-patch, torch 2.9.1+cu128)

**Patched `wrapper.cpp` line emitted:**

```cpp

```

(was: `int64_t s46 = (1.0/1496.0)*arg4_1_size_0;`)

```

issues.title: [inductor] Severe numerical inconsistency: diag_embed + erf + normalize(p=-1) under torch.compile(dynamic=True) — max diff up to 565,248
issues.author: lijunqiang123
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

A model combining Conv2d → BatchNorm2d → ReLU → diag_embed → erf → normalize(p=-1) produces wildly incorrect outputs under torch.compile(dynamic=True) compared to eager mode. The maximum absolute difference reaches 565,248 , indicating a severe correctness bug — not a precision issue, but a fundamentally wrong computation.

Both modes complete without errors and produce identically-shaped outputs. The bug is reproducible across multiple runs with varying random inputs, always producing massive discrepancies.

### Minimal repro
```
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.set_grad_enabled(False)

class Model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(3, 8, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(8)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.conv1(x)
        x = self.bn1(x)
        x = F.relu(x)
        x = torch.diag_embed(x)
        x = torch.erf(x)
        x = F.normalize(x, p=-1, dim=-1)
        return x

model = Model()
x = torch.randn(2, 3, 16, 16)

res_eager = model(*[x])
res_compiled = torch.compile(model, dynamic=True)(x)

print("Max diff:", (res_eager - res_compiled).abs().max().item())
```
### Result (3 consecutive runs, same repro)
```
Run 1: Max diff: 483328.0
Run 2: Max diff: 565248.0
Run 3: Max diff: 528384.0
```
The discrepancy is not deterministic (varies with random input) but always present and massive (5e+05 range). The outputs have identical shape but fundamentally different values.

### Root cause hypothesis
The operator chain creates a numerically fragile computation:

1. `diag_embed` — creates sparse-structured tensors with many near-zero elements
2. `erf` — maps to (-1, 1), further compressing the dynamic range
3. `normalize(p=-1)` — divides by `min(|x|)` along the last dimension, making the result extremely sensitive to tiny values
Under `dynamic=True` , Inductor's fusion of `diag_embed + erf` may produce slightly different intermediate values for near-zero diagonal elements. The `normalize(p=-1)` then amplifies these tiny differences into massive output discrepancies due to division by a near-zero denominator.

### Additional context
- Both eager and compiled modes complete without error — silent correctness bug (INCON type).
- The max diff is 350× larger than a previously reported INCON bug involving polygamma + cumulative_trapezoid (~1,400), suggesting a different root cause.

Under `torch.compile(dynamic=True)` , a model combining Conv2d → GroupNorm → polygamma → cumulative_trapezoid produces numerically incorrect outputs compared to eager mode, despite both completing without errors. The maximum absolute difference is `1420.2` , indicating a correctness bug in Inductor's lowering or fusion for this operator combination.

Eager and compiled outputs have the same shape but contain drastically different values — the compiler silently produces wrong results without any error or warning.

### Minimal repro
```
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

torch.set_grad_enabled(False)

class Model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(3, 16, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.gn1 = nn.GroupNorm(num_groups=4, num_channels=16)

- `torch.polygamma(0, x)` — the digamma function, polygamma of order 0
- `torch.cumulative_trapezoid(x)` — cumulative trapezoidal integration

1. An incorrect decomposition or fusion of `polygamma` with surrounding ops
2. A numerically unstable approximation in `cumulative_trapezoid` under symbolic dimensions

@lijunqiang123 — great questions. Here are some recommendations:

**1. Recommended practices for numerical stability near digamma's poles**

The digamma function (`polygamma(0, x)`) has poles at all non-positive integers (0, -1, -2, ...). Near these poles, the function behaves like `-1/x`, so even tiny floating-point perturbations in the input get amplified enormously. In your case, `x + 0.1` can land values within ~1e-5 of zero after GroupNorm normalizes to near-zero values, and at that point a 1-ULP difference in fp32 (~2e-8) produces output differences of `1/(x)² ≈ 1e10` in the derivative — which is why you see such large absolute errors.

Practical mitigations:

- **Clamp away from the pole:** The simplest and most robust fix is to clamp the input away from the singularity before calling `polygamma`:
  ```python
  eps = 1e-4  # or even 1e-3, depending on your tolerance
  x = torch.clamp(x + 0.1, min=eps)
  x = torch.polygamma(0, x)
  ```
  This bounds the maximum possible output magnitude and eliminates the sensitivity to floating-point roundoff.

- **Use `torch.digamma` with softplus-shifted inputs:** If you need the input to remain differentiable (for training), you can use `F.softplus` to ensure inputs are strictly positive:
  ```python
  x = torch.digamma(F.softplus(x) + eps)
  ```
  `softplus(x) > 0` always, so you never approach the pole.

- **Use `torch.special.digamma` on `abs(x) + offset`:** If the sign of the input doesn't carry semantic meaning for your use case, mapping through `abs()` plus a positive offset avoids the negative-integer poles entirely.

- **Use higher precision for the sensitive computation:** If you need maximum accuracy and can tolerate the cost, cast to float64 around the sensitive region:
  ```python
  x_64 = (x + 0.1).double()
  x = torch.polygamma(0, x_64).float()
  ```

**2. General principle**

This isn't a `torch.compile` bug per se — it's that `torch.compile` is allowed to reorder/fuse floating-point operations in ways that produce results differing by normal fp32 roundoff (~1 ULP). For well-conditioned functions this is invisible, but for ill-conditioned functions like digamma near a pole, any roundoff gets amplified catastrophically. The same issue would appear with different hardware, different CUDA versions, or even different thread scheduling in eager mode on some operators.

The general rule: **if your function has condition number > 1/ε_machine at some input, you must keep inputs away from that region** — no compiler or precision mode can save you otherwise.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

When compiling a function containing `F.interpolate`, `F.conv2d`, `F.max_pool2d`, and `torch.where` using `torch.compile(backend="inductor")`, the forward pass matches eager mode perfectly, but the gradients in the backward pass are completely incorrect (showing massive max diffs).

### Reproducer

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


def inner(x, weight, bias):
    y = F.interpolate(
        x,
        scale_factor=(1.5, 1.25),
        mode="bilinear",
        align_corners=False,
    )
    y = y[:, :, 1:7, 1:8]

    conv = F.conv2d(y, weight, bias, padding=1)
    pool = F.max_pool2d(conv, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1)
    threshold = pool.mean(dim=(2, 3), keepdim=True)
    return conv, pool, threshold


def make_mask(x, weight, bias):
    conv, _, threshold = inner(x, weight, bias)
    return conv > threshold


def fn(x, weight, bias, mask):
    conv, pool, _ = inner(x, weight, bias)

    return torch.where(mask, conv, pool)


def clone_inputs(xs):
    return [x.detach().clone().requires_grad_(True) for x in xs]


def run(f, xs, mask):
    out = f(*xs, mask)
    out.sum().backward()
    return out.detach(), [x.grad.detach().clone() for x in xs]


def max_diff(a, b):
    return (a - b).abs().max().item()


def main():
    print("torch:", torch.__version__)
    print("cuda:", torch.version.cuda)

    torch.manual_seed(0)
    device = "cpu"

    inputs = [
        torch.randn(2, 3, 6, 7, device=device, requires_grad=True),
        torch.randn(4, 3, 3, 3, device=device, requires_grad=True),
        torch.zeros(4, device=device, requires_grad=True),

    inputs_comp = clone_inputs(inputs)

    mask_comp = compiled_mask(*inputs_comp).detach()

    torch._dynamo.reset()

issues.title: [Inductor] Forward output mismatch between Eager and Inductor for F.softshrink with bfloat16 and float scalar
issues.author: xyt66665000
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When applying `torch.nn.functional.softshrink` on a `bfloat16` CUDA tensor with a float scalar `lambd`, the output of `torch.compile(backend="inductor")` does not match the output of Eager mode. 

Based on the numerical results, Eager mode appears to cast the scalar `lambd` (e.g., `9.99`) to `bfloat16` (`10.0`) before the computation, yielding `-10.0625 + 10.0 = -0.0625`. However, Inductor yields `-0.072265625`, indicating a discrepancy in how the scalar type casting or precision is handled during the kernel execution.

This appears related to #185470, but it is not the same reproducer: #185470 reports F.threshold and says softshrink is fixed, while this reproducer shows F.softshrink itself still mismatches eager for the arithmetic result.

### Error logs
```text
(torch-nightly) xyt19@Oasis:/tmp$ python bug.py
Eager     : -0.0625
Inductor  : -0.072265625

 Bug
```

### Minified repro
```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def test_softshrink_mismatch():
    x = torch.tensor([-10.0625], dtype=torch.bfloat16, device="cuda")
    lambd = 9.99  

    def fn(x):
        return F.softshrink(x, lambd)

    eager_out = fn(x)
    
    fn_opt = torch.compile(fn, backend="inductor")
    inductor_out = fn_opt(x)

    print("Eager     :", eager_out.item())       
    print("Inductor  :", inductor_out.item())    
    
    if not torch.allclose(eager_out, inductor_out):
        print("\n Bug")
    else:
        print("\n PASS")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_softshrink_mismatch()
```

### Expected behavior
The forward output of `torch.compile` (Inductor) should strictly match the output of Eager mode.

comments.author: subramanya-dev
comments.body: Hello, I’d like to contribute to this issue. Could a maintainer please assign it to me?

comments.author: jjppp
comments.body:
using `device="cpu"` also gives `-0.072265625`. I think the actual deviation comes from the CUDA implementation of softshrink.
Unlike the CUDA implementation in `aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/ActivationSoftshrinkKernel.cu`, using `device="cpu"` and `"inductor"` upcast `torch.bfloat16` elements to `float` before subtracting or adding `lambd` (for precsiion reasons, maybe?). This makes the CUDA kernel less precise than the others.

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/99f0065df79445bfe7c4aa11fdc20c8d48cf2db9/aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/Activation.cpp#L649-L651

comments.author: krastogi-in
comments.body: I do not fully agree with @jjppp — changing the CUDA eager kernel to compute in float32 would violate PyTorch's type promotion rule that Python scalars do not promote a tensor's dtype. The correct fix is the other direction: casting lambd to the tensor's dtype before computation, matching CUDA eager's existing behavior.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

When compiling a function containing `F.interpolate`, `F.unfold`, and `F.grid_sample` with `torch.compile(backend="inductor", dynamic=True)`, the compilation fails with an `InductorError`. 

The traceback points to torch/_inductor/ir.py in get_stride_order while sorting symbolic strides.

### A Repro
```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def target_function(x, shift, g2_x, g2_pw, g2_b, g2_fw, g3_x, g3_shift, g4_rolled, g4_cw, g4_cb, 
                    g5_x, g5_shift, g7_x, g7_shift, g8_x, g8_shift, g9_x, g9_aff, g9_crop, 
                    g10_x, g10_off, g10_pw, g10_pb, g10_blend, g1_crop, g6_cw, g6_cb):
    
    resized = F.interpolate(x, scale_factor=[1.5, 1.25], mode='bilinear', align_corners=False)
    
    patches = F.unfold(g2_x, kernel_size=3, padding=1, stride=1).transpose(1, 2).contiguous()
    proj = torch.einsum('blp,op->blo', patches, g2_pw) + g2_b.view(1, 1, -1)
    restored = torch.einsum('blo,po->blp', F.gelu(proj), g2_fw).transpose(1, 2).contiguous()
    norm = F.fold(torch.ones_like(restored), output_size=[6, 7], kernel_size=3, padding=1, stride=1).clamp_min(1.0)
    g2_call = F.fold(restored, output_size=[6, 7], kernel_size=3, padding=1, stride=1) / norm

    g3_call = F.interpolate(g3_x, scale_factor=[1.5, 1.25], mode='bilinear', align_corners=False)
    g5_call = F.interpolate(g5_x, scale_factor=[1.5, 1.25], mode='bilinear', align_corners=False)
    g7_call = F.interpolate(g7_x, scale_factor=[1.5, 1.25], mode='bilinear', align_corners=False)
    g8_call = F.interpolate(g8_x, scale_factor=[1.5, 1.25], mode='bilinear', align_corners=False)

    conv4 = F.conv2d(g4_rolled[:, :, 1:7, 1:8], g4_cw, g4_cb, padding=1)
    pool4 = F.max_pool2d(conv4, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1)
    g4_call = torch.where(conv4 > pool4.mean(dim=[2, 3], keepdim=True), conv4, pool4)

    res9 = F.interpolate(F.pad(g9_x, [1, 2, 2, 1], 'reflect'), scale_factor=1.5, mode='bicubic', align_corners=False)
    grid9 = F.affine_grid(g9_aff, size=[2, 3, 13, 15], align_corners=False)
    g9_call = F.grid_sample(res9, grid9, mode='bilinear', padding_mode='reflection', align_corners=False)

comments.body:
I looked into the root cause. The crash is in stride-order computation, and it reduces to symbolic strides being compared with a non-symbolic-aware sort.

The failing path (from the 2.13 nightly traceback in this issue):
graph.py:2010   ir.get_stride_order(strides)
ir.py:345       get_fill_order(seq, shape_env)
ir.py:320       argsort(seq)
utils.py:1451   sorted(a_r, key=getter, reverse=True)   # getter = seq.__getitem__
sympy/relational.py:519  __bool__  ->  TypeError
argsort sorts indices using the raw stride values as the key:

def argsort(seq):
     >> getter = seq.__getitem__
      >>a_r = range(len(seq))
      >>return list(sorted(a_r, key=getter, reverse=True))

With dynamic=True, the entries of seq are SymPy expressions (here s53). When sorted compares two symbolic strides, expr_a < expr_b does not evaluate to a Python bool — it returns a sympy.
Relational. sorted then calls bool() on that relational, and SymPy raises:
TypeError: cannot determine truth value of Relational: 1 < s53

The key observation: get_fill_order has the shape_env (it is passed in at ir.py:345 as get_fill_order(seq, shape_env)), but it calls argsort(seq) without it. So the one piece of context needed to resolve the symbolic comparison — via size hints / statically_known_* — is dropped at the argsort boundary. argsort then falls back to a raw <, which is undefined for symbolic strides.

This is a persistent issue, not a regression. 
I see the same failure was reported in #172204 (Jan 2026, torch 2.9.1) on a ViT block — identical path (get_stride_order -> get_fill_order(seq, shape_env) -> argsort(seq) -> SymPy __bool__), with cannot determine truth value of Relational: 768*((s53//16))**2 < 12. Same root cause, different model, ~4 months apart. 
The minimal ViT repro in #172204 is smaller than the one here and may be more convenient for bisecting; 
this issue (interpolate/unfold/grid_sample) and #172204 (attention + conv patch-embed) appear to be the same bug surfaced through different ops that produce symbolic strides.


Fix direction: the stride sort needs to be symbolic-aware. The natural fix consistent with the rest of Inductor would be to thread shape_env into the sort and resolve the comparison through the existing size-hint machinery (e.g. ordering by size_hint / statically_known_true, adding the corresponding guard) rather than relying on raw <. I did not want to send a blind patch into stride ordering since a wrong comparator can silently change layout decisions — happy to put together a fix with tests if a maintainer can confirm the preferred approach (thread shape_env into argsort vs. resolve hints in get_fill_order before sorting).

Repro confirmed conceptually against both tracebacks; 

I do not have a CUDA box to verify a patch end-to-end, which is why I am sharing the diagnosis rather than a PR.
